sections.title: What you already know
sections.content: You know *mientras* "while" from A2 Unit 13: two actions happen at the same time, with the indicative (*Mientras cocinaba, escuchaba música*). It works the same way in the present: *Mientras trabajo, escucho música*. Both actions are facts. New here: *mientras* + subjunctive means "as long as". The speaker looks ahead and says that something will go on for as long as another thing is true, and it may or may not stay true.

sections.title: While or as long as?
rows: While I cook, you listen to music. (Two facts at once: indicative.)
While we were waiting, it started to rain. (Past: indicative.)
Mientras dure la lluvia, nos quedamos aquí.
As long as the rain lasts, we'll stay here. (Duration: subjunctive.)
Puedes quedarte mientras no hagas ruido.
You can stay as long as you don't make noise. (Condition: subjunctive.)
Ana habla mucho, mientras que Luis casi no habla.
Ana talks a lot, whereas Luis hardly talks. (Contrast: indicative.)

sections.title: Two shades of "as long as"
sections.content: With the subjunctive, *mientras* can measure time (*mientras dure la lluvia*: for as long as the rain lasts) or set a condition (*mientras no hagas ruido*). The second use means the same as *siempre que* "provided that". You know *siempre que* from B1 Unit 21. In both, the subjunctive tells the listener that the situation is not a fact yet.

items.spanish: Mientras dure la tormenta, nos quedamos en el café.
items.english: As long as the storm lasts, we'll stay in the café.

items.spanish: Te presto mi coche mientras lo cuides.
items.english: I'll lend you my car as long as you look after it.

items.spanish: Mientras tenga trabajo, no pienso mudarme.
items.english: As long as I have work, I don't plan to move.

items.spanish: Mientras esperábamos el autobús, empezó a llover.
items.english: While we were waiting for the bus, it started to rain.

sections.content: Ask what the speaker means. Two things going on together, now or in the past: indicative. "For as long as" or "on condition that": subjunctive. English uses the plain present for both (*while I cook*, *as long as it lasts*), so Spanish makes the difference with the mood.
